prerequisites: It is desirable that students taking Thermal Engineering I have passed Physics (I and II), Chemistry, and Mathematics (I and II) subjects, as effective follow-up of this subject will be practically impossible without the establishment of the prior concepts provided by these subjects.

learning_outcomes.text: Understanding and interpretation of texts and data, development of skills for their concretization and their clear and concise exposition.
Aptitude for the distribution of resources and time and their implementation in real situations.
Ability to transmit concepts, ideas, processes, etc., related to Industrial Engineering orally and in writing, clearly and correctly.
Ability to use scientific-technical tools for solving calculation and design problems in Industrial Engineering and aptitude for finding sustainable engineering solutions.
Ability to work together and ability to develop multidisciplinary projects.
Ability to relate to other people and an open attitude towards creating new relationships.
Ability to incorporate new knowledge in the area of Industrial Engineering, based on the acquired training and necessary for the evolution of technique.
Knowledge of applied thermodynamics and heat transfer. Basic principles and their application to solving engineering problems.

syllabus_topics: Introduction, objectives and fundamental concepts. Units.
First Principle of Thermodynamics in control volumes. Heat exchangers and boilers.
Analysis of thermodynamic processes with Termograf.
Determination of thermodynamic properties of a pure substance.
Determination of the ratio of specific heats for air.
Analysis of the variables involved in a transient process of filling and emptying an air tank using a compressor.
teaching_methods: Introductory activities (directed by the professor) placing the student in objectives, methodologies, and techniques.
Master class: transmission of knowledge, with continuous interaction between professor and students, attendance recommended.
Scientific events: inviting speakers for conferences, programming extraordinary courses, recommending attendance to congresses/exhibitions related to the subject.
Classroom practices: problem-solving and simulations using computer programs, requiring students to have software installed and internet access.
Laboratory practices: hands-on experiments synchronized with theoretical topics, subject to material and budget availability.
External practices: organized visits to companies, entities, or institutions related to the course content, when circumstances allow.
Seminars: to address general deficiencies, conceptual errors, or expand knowledge on related topics not covered in the main program.
Exhibitions: voluntary construction and display of posters related to the course themes.
Tutorials: personalized attention to guide students in resolving difficulties after attempting to solve them independently.
Online monitoring activities: professor's website for comments and a forum for discussion.
Problem-solving: students independently solve problems similar to exams, organized in progressively increasing difficulty.
Case studies: responding to specific situations, potentially related to social events.
Discussion forums: external forum allowing intervention from professionals in related fields, fostering discussion and learning.

assessment_methods.method: Written exam (usually comprising three or four problems)

assessment_rules: All exercises in exams have equal value unless specified. An exercise is correct if the correct result is reached, or if calculation/reading errors lead to a non-absurd result (or an absurd one recognized by the student). Chained questions are evaluated independently unless the preceding answer is manifestly absurd and not recognized. Grades are awarded on a scale of 0-10: Fail (<5), Pass (5-6.9), Good (7-8.9), Excellent (9-10).
